newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Korean Merchant banks borrow.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Korean Merchant banks borrow.

text.p: A couple of South Korean merchant banks made their move on Wednesday with new issues, while Tingyi Holdings formally launched its big FRN.
Bankers also took a closer look at APP Global Finance's US$500 million deal, which was presented in Hong Kong today.
Kyongnam Bank brought its US$50 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue. The certificates have a final maturity of five years but can be put or called after three.
The deal pays a margin of 45 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate and with fees an all-in return of 50 basis points to the top tier.
Arrangers are KDB Asia, LTCB Asia, Merrill Lynch Far East and Standard Chartered Investment Banking.
Hansol Merchant also launched an FRCD. The US$30 million deal has a final maturity of three years and annual puts.
It pays a margin of 49.5 basis points over LIBOR and an all-in return of 52.5 basis points to the first put.

The arrangers pointed out that by putting the issue in the first year lenders benefit from the reduced BIS capital reserve requirement. The paper will be redeemed at 99.7 if put in year one and at 99.775 if put in year two.
The transaction carries an ownership covenant stipulating that Hansol Paper Co must retain at least 30 percent direct ownership of the borrower.

Bankers said the issues may be a difficult sell. These banks are not as popular as the large commercial banks, despite the more attractive spread. Moreover, supply of South Korean paper is on the rise again, bankers said.
Kyangju Bank is expected to launch its US$50 million FRCD on Friday. Other merchant banks in the market are Kumho, Saehan, Hyundai International Merchant Bank and Asian Banking Corp.
Add to those Boram Bank and Cho Hung Bank and the list starts to get very long.
Hanil Hong Kong is doing something a little different with a Hong Kong dollar deal in the works.
Recent Korean corporate issues haven't fared very well, a result that some bankers attribute to unfavorable events.
Daewoo's last syndication wasn't helped by the conviction of Daewoo Group chairman Kim Woo-choong on charges of bribing former South Korean president Roh Tae-woo.
Similarly, U.S. missile attacks on Iraq scared banks away from Hyundai Engineering's recent transaction because the company has significant interests in Iraq, one banker explained.
Elsewhere, Tingyi Holdings formally launched its US$150 million floating rate note via arranger ING Barings. The company is Hong Kong-listed, Taiwan-owned and China-based.
While some bankers said they do not want to take on China risk, others said Tingyi, a giant in the instant noodle market, is an attractive credit at the deal's price.
The three-year notes pay a margin of 110 basis points over LIBOR and an all-in return of 125 basis points.
APP Global Finance held a roadshow for its US$500 million secured FRN in Hong Kong today.

The funds ultimately will be used by Asia Pulp and Paper, which has no direct or indirect ownership interest in the borrower. The transaction has been structured to maximize tax benefits in Singapore, where Asia Pulp and Paper is headquartered, and to help lower the company's gearing ratio.

Some bankers have expressed reservations about the deal, which is secured by Asia Pulp and Paper shares rather than fixed assets. But others said they like Asia Pulp and Paper's story and are planning to take a closer look at the issue.
The roadshows, so far held in Taipei, Seoul and Hong Kong, have been well attended and some of the paper has been placed. Presentations will be held in Singapore and Zurich.
